\begin{abstract}
\noindent
This is the Week~5 report for the QSVM track. Three of its results revise
conclusions this track had previously drawn rather than merely extending them.
First, the classical baseline is no longer SVM alone: on EMBER binary a random
forest beats SVM at every \nc{}, so the quantum--classical margins reported up to
now were \emph{understated}. Second, the collapse of the QSVM to chance
performance on the CIC 15-class task, previously recorded as unexplained, is
attributed here to \emph{kernel concentration} and demonstrated against an RBF
control on identical features. Third, all cross-framework claims are now
supported by paired significance tests, which had been specified in Week~1 and
never run: all 84 testable comparisons favour the classical model at $p < 0.05$.
We also close the subsample-representativeness validation that every quantum
result in this project had silently assumed for four weeks.
\end{abstract}

\section{Data and protocol}
\label{sec:data}

Two malware datasets, each carrying a binary and a 15-class task.

\begin{description}[leftmargin=1.2em,style=nextline]
\item[CIC-MalMem-2022] Obfuscated-malware memory dumps, 55 numeric
forensic features (process, handle, callback and DLL counts). The binary task
uses all \num{58596} rows and is exactly balanced between benign and malware. The
15-class task drops benign rows --- detecting benign is the binary task's job ---
leaving \num{29298} malware rows across 15 families, mildly imbalanced at
$1.7\times$ between the largest and smallest.
\item[EMBER 2018] Static PE features, 2381 dimensions. Work is done on a
\num{18014}-row extract of the published test set; the full set is a single
$200\,000 \times 2384$ block that cannot be read incrementally. The binary task
uses all \num{18014} rows and is $88.9\%$ malware. The 15-class task keeps
families with at least 500 samples, caps at the 15 largest, and downsamples each
to the smallest kept count, giving \num{14325} rows exactly balanced at 955 per
family.
\end{description}

\paragraph{Shared evaluation.} The quantum kernel costs $O(n^2)$ circuit
evaluations to build, so every quantum result is computed on a stratified
1000-row subsample rather than the full data. The subsample and the five
stratified outer folds computed over it are written to disk by the quantum
runner and \emph{replayed} by the classical runner, so both frameworks are
scored on identical rows and identical folds --- 800 training and 200 held-out
rows per fold. \S\ref{sec:repr} verifies that this subsample is faithful to its
population.

Both frameworks also consume one shared feature pipeline: a zero-variance
filter, a correlation filter at $0.95$, standardisation, then PCA to \nc{}
components. That single parameter fixes the classical feature count and the
quantum qubit budget simultaneously, and is what makes the comparison
like-for-like. The pipeline is fit on training-fold rows only.

\paragraph{Metric.} All results are held-out macro-F1, the unweighted mean of
per-class F1, reported as a mean over the five outer folds. Accuracy is not used
as a headline: on EMBER binary at \nc{}~$=1$ the QSVM attains $0.890$ accuracy
in three of five folds while the benign class's F1 is exactly $0.000$ in those
same folds, because $88.9\%$ of rows are malware and the model labels everything
malware. Accuracy there reports near-success for a classifier that never once
identifies the class of interest.

\section{Subsample representativeness}
\label{sec:repr}

Every quantum result in this project is computed on a 1000-row stratified
subsample, forced by the $O(n^2)$ kernel cost. That the subsample represents its
population was specified as a Week~2 task, never executed, and assumed for four
weeks. It is now measured.

The decisive statistic is the two-sample Kolmogorov--Smirnov rejection count read
\emph{against its own null expectation}, since a perfectly faithful subsample
still produces about $\alpha \cdot n_{\mathrm{features}}$ rejections by chance.
A bare count is uninterpretable; the ratio is not.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.55\textwidth]{figures/fig_representativeness.pdf}
\caption{Per-feature KS rejections at $\alpha = 0.05$, subsample against full
population, beside what chance alone produces. CIC rejects nothing where
$\approx 2.75$ were expected; EMBER rejects one feature where $\approx 119$
were expected. Maximum class-proportion drift is below $0.001$ on both.}
\label{fig:repr}
\end{figure}

Both subsamples are faithful. Four weeks of quantum results now rest on a
measured foundation rather than an assumption.

\section{Why CIC 15-class collapses}
\label{sec:kernel}

That summary established the contrast --- the QSVM sits at the random baseline on CIC
15-class while reaching $0.42$--$0.52$ on EMBER 15-class --- and ruled out class
imbalance and qubit count, closing with ``the actual cause is unidentified''.
Two measurements now separate a dataset effect from a kernel effect.

\subsection{Feature geometry explains the dataset, not the kernel}

Measured on the identical projected features both frameworks consume, fit on
training folds only: EMBER's families are $\approx 8\times$ more separable by
one-vs-rest Fisher ratio, and up to $50\times$ on the worst-case family. CIC's
silhouette coefficient is \emph{negative at every} \nc{}: the average CIC point
lies closer to another family's centroid than to its own.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig_geometry.pdf}
\caption{Class separability of the shared PCA projection, averaged over the five
outer folds. Both metrics are scale-invariant and therefore comparable across
datasets of very different dimensionality.}
\label{fig:geom}
\end{figure}

Counter-intuitively, CIC's PCA explains substantially \emph{more} variance
($33$--$81\%$) than EMBER's ($8$--$30\%$) while separating families far less ---
CIC's variance is concentrated in directions that do not discriminate family,
which is plausible for a memory-forensics feature vector whose process and
handle counts track workload rather than malware family.

This explains why \emph{every} method does badly on CIC 15-class. It cannot
explain the QSVM-specific failure, because a classical SVM extracts
$0.108$--$0.165$ macro-F1 from exactly these features where the QSVM extracts
$0.056$--$0.079$.

\subsection{Kernel geometry explains the kernel}

The decisive experiment builds a classical RBF Gram matrix on the \emph{identical}
feature matrix, which separates ``these features are hard'' from ``this kernel is
bad''. Both diagnostics are computed on the first outer training fold at
\nc{}~$=6$ with the IQP encoding ($800$ rows, $6$ qubits).

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig_kernel_diagnostics.pdf}
\caption{(a)~Standard deviation of the off-diagonal Gram entries: as this
collapses, the Gram approaches a scaled identity and the SVM has nothing to
separate on. (b)~Kernel-target alignment relative to its floor. A constant
kernel scores $1/\sqrt{15} \approx 0.258$ on 15 balanced classes, so the raw
alignment is nearly uninformative and the excess is what carries meaning.}
\label{fig:kernel}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Alignment separates the datasets, not the kernels.}
On CIC the fidelity kernel lands $0.000069$ \emph{below} the constant-kernel
floor --- indistinguishable from an all-ones matrix --- and the RBF control is
below it too. On EMBER both clear it by $\approx 0.03$.

\paragraph{Concentration separates the kernels, specifically on CIC.}
The RBF kernel produces near-identical spread on both datasets ($0.2212$ against
$0.2184$, a $1\%$ difference), so CIC's features do not make a classical kernel
concentrate. The fidelity kernel tracks RBF on EMBER ($0.92\times$) but collapses
to $\mathbf{0.40\times}$ its spread on CIC. Every off-diagonal similarity is
squeezed into a band $2.5\times$ narrower from the same inputs.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.55\textwidth]{figures/fig_concentration_sweep.pdf}
\caption{Concentration across the full 15-class sweep. This required no new
computation: the estimator has logged the off-diagonal spread on every fit since
Week~2. EMBER's Gram is $1.9$--$2.6\times$ more spread than CIC's at every
comparable setting, and concentration worsens with qubit count on both --- the
trend the \texttt{bandwidth} parameter exists to counteract.}
\label{fig:conc}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{A tension we state rather than resolve.}
Alignment reports that neither kernel's Gram carries label information on CIC,
yet a classical SVM reaches $0.16$ there. Kernel-target alignment is a global,
unweighted average over all pairs, and an SVM requires no such thing --- it
requires support vectors, a regularisation constant and class weights, none of
which alignment models. Alignment is a useful measure of relative dataset
difficulty and an unreliable predictor of achievable SVM performance. The
concentration result does not share this weakness, because it describes the Gram
the SVM actually receives.

\paragraph{What is and is not supported.}
Supported: the fidelity kernel's failure on CIC is a property of \emph{the
kernel}, not of the dataset. Not supported: that tuning \texttt{bandwidth} would
repair it. Bandwidth is the identified mechanism and has never been tuned on CIC
beyond its default, but no sweep was run. This is a hypothesis with a named
lever, not a measured fix.

\section{Paired significance tests}
\label{sec:sig}

Significance testing was specified in Week~1, built and unit-tested, and never
run. Four weeks of ``QSVM loses to classical'' rested on differences in mean
macro-F1 with no test that any gap exceeded fold-to-fold noise.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.58\textwidth]{figures/fig_significance.pdf}
\caption{Effect size against paired $t$-test $p$-value for all 84 testable
quantum--classical pairs. Every point lies left of $p = 0.05$ and above zero:
all 84 favour the classical model at conventional significance. The worst
$p$-value across every pair is $0.0241$.}
\label{fig:sig}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Wilcoxon returned $0.0625$ for all 84 pairs, and that is not a null result}

With five paired samples, the Wilcoxon signed-rank test's smallest attainable
two-sided $p$-value is $0.0625$. It is therefore \emph{mathematically incapable}
of reaching $p < 0.05$ at this fold count, regardless of effect size. All 84
pairs returning exactly $0.0625$ means every pair achieved the most extreme rank
configuration available --- all five folds favouring the classical model.
Reporting ``Wilcoxon found nothing significant'' would be a serious misreading.
Raising the fold count to six would put $0.03125$ within reach; that, not a
different test, is the remedy.

\subsection{What could not be tested}

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{All CIC binary comparisons} (9 cells $\times$ 4 models). Every CIC
binary run --- classical \emph{and} quantum, 45 fold records per model --- was
logged before the experiment tracker recorded parent/child run structure, and
carries no recoverable sweep boundary. The raw records show the QSVM at
$0.92$--$1.00$ macro-F1, consistent with the earlier ``ties on binary'' reading,
but they resolve into two distinct sweeps per \nc{} with different
configurations and no identifier separating them. Grouping them by time-gap
clustering would invent a boundary the data does not record; no attempt was
made. The limitation is symmetric across frameworks, not a quantum-specific gap.
\item \textbf{McNemar between frameworks.} The test needs per-sample predictions
from both models on a shared test set. QSVM predictions were not persisted
during these sweeps. Persistence has since been added, but no sweep was re-run,
so nothing is recoverable retroactively. Classical-versus-classical McNemar was
run: on EMBER 15-class the random forest beats XGBoost at $p = 0.0022$, while on
CIC 15-class \emph{no pair separates at all} --- consistent with
\S\ref{sec:kernel}.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{A methodological note on selecting comparable runs}

Identifying which logged records constitute one cross-validation run is not
mechanical, and getting it wrong silently corrupts every aggregate. Filtering on
$(\text{dataset}, \text{task}, \nc{}, \text{model}, \text{encoding})$ --- the
obvious approach --- fails twice over:

\begin{enumerate}
\item The same configuration has legitimately been swept several times over the
project's weeks, so a parameter-based grouping returns 10, 15 or 20 records for
a five-fold sweep and averages distinct hyperparameter searches together. Of the
parameter groups in the experiment export, 57 have a size other than five.
\item For the QSVM, \emph{encoding is a per-fold outcome, not a configuration
key}: the two-tier tuner selects the winning encoding inside each fold, so a
single joint sweep can appear as ``four angle folds and one IQP fold''. Grouping
on encoding splits one sweep into two incomplete ones.
\end{enumerate}

Runs are therefore grouped by parent run, keeping only sweeps whose parent
completed with exactly five folds; where several clean sweeps match, the most
recent wins. Under this rule the store holds 125 nested sweeps, 123 of them
clean. The two exceptions --- an interrupted sweep and a truncated three-fold
sweep from a past out-of-memory incident --- are excluded automatically rather
than deleted, leaving the history intact.

\section{SOREL-20M closed}
\label{sec:sorel}

SOREL-20M is closed for this track rather than deferred. Its multiclass
labelling scheme was designed and validated over 19.7M rows and remains
delivered work; the feature store was never fetched and \emph{no SOREL sweep was
ever run}. The two are independent, and the labelling report should not be read
as partial results.

Measured at close-out: \SI{227}{\gibi\byte} of free disk against a
\SI{71.6}{\gibi\byte} requirement, so disk is not the blocker. Memory is not
either --- the store is a memory-mapped LMDB whose reads page through the
operating system cache, which the earlier phrasing (``the whole file must be
local before any row can be read'') is easy to misread as a memory constraint.
It is a locality constraint. The blocker is the fixed \SI{71.6}{\gibi\byte}
transfer, unavoidable because LMDB offers no key-level remote access: there is
no way to fetch only the thousand rows a sweep would need.

\section{Summary}

The project's central claim is stronger than it was and points the same way.
Classical models beat the QSVM on every testable configuration, now with
$p < 0.05$ on all 84 of them rather than on mean differences alone, and the
EMBER margins turn out to have been understated rather than overstated. The one
configuration where the quantum pipeline was ever competitive --- CIC binary ---
cannot be significance-tested from what was logged, and we say so rather than
quietly dropping it.

What is genuinely new is the mechanism. The fidelity kernel does not fail on CIC
because CIC's features are hard: a classical RBF kernel on the identical
features does not concentrate. It fails because the fidelity kernel itself
collapses to $0.40\times$ the classical kernel's spread on that data. That is a
statement about the method rather than about the dataset, and it is the most
transferable result this track has produced.

\paragraph{Reproduction.} Every figure is generated programmatically from
the same recorded experiment metrics the tables are drawn from, so no figure can
disagree with a reported number. The implementation carries 144 passing tests.
